links.basis: The budget report's community profile attributes population, private dwellings and median age to the 2024 Municipal Census by name, and the per-capita spending metric Council is asked to judge the budget by is computed from that population.
The same community profile attributes median household income to the 2021 Federal Census by name. The municipal census does not collect income, so the federal one fills the gap.

Local Government Fiscal Framework funding appears as a named capital funding source in the 2026 budget at $8,401,000, 18.4% of the capital plan, and is carried forward at $8,317,000 a year across the five-year capital forecast. Named road rehabilitation programs are funded from it directly.

The budget benchmarks ten years of tax increases and per-capita spending against Alberta CPI, quoted at 25.9% cumulatively. Context for the fiscal argument rather than a computational input, hence a citation rather than a calculation.

The monthly CPI releases are produced according to the concepts, classifications, sampling, price collection, index calculation and basket-update methods documented in the Canadian CPI Reference Paper. The document states: "For further information on the concepts and use of the CPI, see The Canadian Consumer Price Index Reference Paper (Catalogue number 62-553-X)."

The Canadian Consumer Price Index Reference Paper (catalogue 62-553-X) Chapter 4 states the three criteria the CPI product and geographical classifications are designed to meet, and footnotes them directly to 'ILO et al. (2004), paragraph 3.144' — i.e. the Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice, predecessor of the current CPI Manual: Concepts and Methods. The Reference Paper's bibliography lists the manual in full: 'International Labour Office. 2004. Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice.…

Statistics Canada's basket-update methodology paper states under 'Data sources' that 'The updated basket weights were derived primarily using consumer expenditures from the 2025 national Household Final Consumption Expenditure (HFCE) series, replacing those derived from the 2024 national HFCE series.' The CPI is a Laspeyres-type index whose upper-level aggregation weights are exactly these expenditure shares, so HFCE determines the relative influence of every component on headline CPI.

The same 'Data sources' section states that 'Household expenditures reported in the Survey of Household Spending (SHS) are used to supplement the HFCE expenditure data, mainly providing expenditure detail at lower levels of aggregation, including geographic aggregation.' SHS therefore supplies the sub-provincial and detailed-product weight structure that HFCE cannot resolve.
Calgary and Edmonton allocations weight population at 48 per cent, and the fact sheet names Municipal (Census Subdivision) Population Estimates as the data source.
Calgary and Edmonton allocations weight education property tax requisitions at 48 per cent, sourced from the Education Property Tax Requisition Comparison Report.
Allocations to local governments other than Calgary and Edmonton weight population at 65 per cent, taken from the Municipal Affairs Population List.

Tangible capital assets (15 per cent), five-year average cumulative amortization (10 per cent) and length of local roads (10 per cent) are all drawn from named schedules of the Municipal Financial and Statistical Data.
Needs-based funding eligibility is set by comparing a municipality's equalized assessment per capita, or per kilometre of road, against the provincial average.

The LGFF Act sets a Revenue Index Factor comparing provincial revenue three years prior against four years prior, and municipal capital funding rises or falls by exactly that percentage. 2025 funding rose 13.6% to $820 million on the strength of 13.6% revenue growth between 2021-22 and 2022-23.
Aggregate LGFF funding amounts must be communicated to municipalities two years in advance, and are announced through the quarterly fiscal update.

Canadian Government Finance Statistics is one of the seven account categories that make up the CSMA.

The Canadian National Economic Accounts are compiled using SNA 2008 as the organising framework, which supplies the concepts, classifications and methods used to measure production, income, saving and investment.

Found in the same reading of GFSM 2014 that produced the COFOG edge: the Manual's own introduction states its concepts and principles are harmonized with SNA 2008.

Each municipality submits information on every assessable property annually for the audit that determines its equalized assessment. The county's is the same submission as the city's, against a very different mix of property.

The Recording and Reporting Information for Assessment Audit and Equalized Assessment Manual describes an annual submission of data from municipalities to Municipal Affairs containing 'the information about every assessable property in the municipality for the purposes of conducting the annual audit and for determining the equalized assessment'. The province divides the municipality's taxable assessment by its audited assessment level to reach 100% of market value.

The city's roll carries the same regulated classes at much smaller scale — $1.45 million of farmland and $44.4 million of machinery and equipment in Bylaw C-1486 — and they are valued under the same provincial guidelines. The dependency is structural, not proportional to size.

The 2025 Alberta Linear Property Assessment Minister's Guidelines define 'AER means the Alberta Energy Regulator' and then read assessment inputs straight out of its records: for pipelines and wells licensed by the AER 'the assessment must reflect the characteristics and specifications as of October 31 of the assessment year, as contained in the records of the AER'. Pipeline assessment classification codes are set by 'pipeline material, outside diameter, and the maximum operating pressure ... as contained in the…

Nearly 40% of the county's taxable assessment is machinery and equipment and linear property, with farmland on top — all regulated classes. Alberta publishes annual Minister's Guidelines for each, and the assessment regulations require an assessor preparing a regulated assessment to follow the procedures set out in the applicable guideline rather than value at market.
The dataset is compiled from the financial information return and statistical information return submitted annually by every Alberta municipality.

The same statutory requirement that binds the city: each municipality prepares annual audited financial statements and a financial information return, submitted together to Municipal Affairs by May 1.

Municipal Affairs states that the Municipal Government Act requires each municipality to prepare both annual audited financial statements and a financial information return, both returned by May 1, and that 'the completed FIR should be submitted with the signed and dated copy of the audited financial statements'. The FIR is the same year's audited figures restated in the province's standard schedule.

Note 1 states plainly: 'Property tax revenues are based on property tax assessment values provided by the City of Grande Prairie.' The largest revenue line in the statements is the assessment roll multiplied by the rates.

Every statement of operations in the document carries a Budget column beside the actual — net municipal property taxes of $129,935,024 budgeted against $131,071,106 collected. The statements are in part a report card on the budget, so they carry it.

Schedule 3 nets the Alberta School Foundation Fund requisition of $30,181,579 out of gross property taxes to arrive at net municipal property taxes. The notes further explain that over-levies and under-levies against the requisition are accrued and corrected in the following year's requisition rates.

The auditor's report and note 1 both state the statements are prepared in accordance with Canadian public sector accounting standards as established by the Public Sector Accounting Board. The standards decide what the statements are permitted to recognise, which is why this is a methodology dependency rather than a data one.

On 5 May 2020 PSAB approved 'Option 2 - Adapt IPSAS principles when developing future standards' as its International Strategy: PSAB continues to issue Canadian Public Sector Accounting Standards, but future standards are based on the principles in the corresponding IPSAS, and PSAB will only amend an IPSAS principle where it is contrary to PSAB's own Conceptual Framework. PSAB has separately proposed modifying the Canadian public sector GAAP hierarchy in Section PS 1150 to position IPSAS as the go-to framework…
Every operating schedule carries a budget column headed '(Budget - Note 26)' beside the actual — taxation of $154,224,852 budgeted against $152,165,231 collected.

Schedule 3 nets provincial school of $27,396,849 and separate school of $1,249,833 out of gross taxes, noting that the schedule 'also includes requisitions for education and other external organizations that are not part of the municipal reporting entity'.
Schedule 3 nets designated industrial properties of $359,713 actual against $359,764 budgeted.

Schedule 3 nets a senior foundation requisition of $1,054,798 actual against $1,061,836 budgeted. This schedule is also what disambiguates the two requisitions in the tax bylaw, where the PDF's table layout leaves the Grande Spirit and DIP figures adjacent and easy to transpose.

Prepared in accordance with Canadian public sector accounting standards established by the Public Sector Accounting Board. The auditor's other-matter paragraph records that the prior year's statements carried a modified opinion for a departure from those standards on asset retirement obligations — the standard binding in the breach.
The Municipal Affairs Population List is based on municipal census results or federal census data, and federal census counts are used where a municipality has not run its own census.
Municipalities that choose to conduct a census report the results to Municipal Affairs by September 1 and those results are reflected in the population list. The county counted in 2024.

The population list's own usage note: 'The information in the lists is based on municipal census results (Alberta municipalities may choose to conduct a census in any year) or federal census counts. Municipalities that choose to conduct a census are required to report the results to Municipal Affairs by September 1 of that year, and those results are reflected in the population lists.'

Alberta's education property tax page states the mechanism directly: 'Municipal Affairs establishes the provincial mill rate used to determine each municipality's share of the provincial education tax. The provincial equalized assessment base used to determine education property taxes this year reflects 2024 property values.' Alberta's municipal population estimation model is built on a standard methodology drawing on provincial administrative data together with federal government sources, specifically the federal census.
